**PostgreSQL limits to know before sizing the schema and connection pool**

I checked all three answers against the current PostgreSQL documentation on postgresql.org.

**Identifier length.** By default, PostgreSQL uses at most 63 bytes of an identifier, such as a table or column name. The lexical-structure chapter explains that the system uses no more than NAMEDATALEN−1 bytes of an identifier, and that NAMEDATALEN is 64 by default (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-syntax-lexical.html). The appendix of limits gives the same figure, an upper limit of 63 bytes that "can be increased by recompiling PostgreSQL" (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/limits.html). PostgreSQL does not reject a longer name. It truncates it without warning, so two long names that start the same way can end up identical (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-syntax-lexical.html). The limit is in bytes, not characters. Names in a multibyte encoding such as UTF-8 with non-ASCII letters therefore hit it sooner. If you generate names automatically, for example for partitions or foreign-key constraints, check their length in code.

**Columns per table.** A table can have at most 1,600 columns. The same page says the real limit is lower, because a row must fit in a single 8,192-byte heap page (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/limits.html). The documentation's example: 1,600 `int` columns take 6,400 bytes and fit on a page, but 1,600 `bigint` columns take 12,800 bytes and do not. Large variable-length values such as `text` or `varchar` can be moved out of the row into TOAST storage, leaving an 18-byte pointer in the row. Dropped columns still count toward the 1,600 limit (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/limits.html). So a "wide table" design that adds and drops columns over time will slowly use up the limit, even if the visible column count looks small.

**max_connections.** The connection-settings page says the default "is typically 100 connections, but might be less if your kernel settings will not support it (as determined during initdb)." The parameter can only be set at server start, so changing it means a restart (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-connection.html). Don't assume a server has exactly 100. Check the value it actually reports with `SHOW max_connections`. Remember that some connections are kept for superusers and that admin and monitoring tools also use connections. All application pool instances together have to fit in what is left.

**Recommendation.** Keep identifiers well under 63 bytes, and design so that no table comes close to the column limit; for example, move sparse attributes into a child table or a `jsonb` column instead of adding many columns. Size the combined pool across all service replicas below the server's actual `max_connections`, minus reserved and admin connections, and put a pooler such as PgBouncer in front rather than raising `max_connections` far above 100.

**Research note: PostgreSQL memory and WAL defaults on a new install**

Before you change anything on the new PostgreSQL install, here is what the three settings default to. I took each value from the current official PostgreSQL documentation, which is the PostgreSQL 18 manual.

The first setting is work_mem. It sets how much memory a single query operation, such as a sort or a hash table, can use before it starts writing temporary files to disk. The documentation says plainly that "the default value is four megabytes (4MB)" (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-resource.html). The limit applies to each operation, not to each session or the whole server. One complex query can run several sorts and hashes at the same time, and many connections can do this at once. So the total memory used can be many times the work_mem value. Keep that in mind before you raise it across the whole server.

The second setting is shared_buffers. This is the memory the server sets aside for its own shared cache of data pages. The documentation says "the default is typically 128 megabytes (128MB), but might be less if your kernel settings will not support it (as determined during initdb)" (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-resource.html). So 128MB is the usual default, but it is not certain. On a machine with tight kernel shared-memory limits, initdb may have written a lower value into postgresql.conf. Run `SHOW shared_buffers;` on your instance to see what it actually got. The same page notes that changing this setting requires a server restart, so it is best to settle on a value before the server goes into production.

The third setting is max_wal_size. It controls how much write-ahead log (WAL) can build up between automatic checkpoints. Once that much WAL has been written, PostgreSQL triggers a checkpoint. The documentation says "the default is 1 GB" (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-wal.html). The same page says this is a soft limit: "WAL size can exceed max_wal_size under special circumstances, such as heavy load, a failing archive_command or archive_library, or a high wal_keep_size setting" (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-wal.html). In practice, if your workload writes a lot, 1GB of WAL can fill quickly and cause frequent checkpoints. Frequent checkpoints add I/O and produce more full-page writes. Raising max_wal_size spaces checkpoints further apart, but recovery after a crash will take longer and the WAL will use more disk.

To summarize, a new install starts with work_mem = 4MB, shared_buffers = 128MB (sometimes less, depending on the kernel), and max_wal_size = 1GB. These defaults are chosen so PostgreSQL will start on almost any hardware, not to make it fast on a dedicated database server. That is why all three are usually worth revisiting. They affect different things: work_mem is memory per operation and can multiply, shared_buffers is one fixed cache for the whole server and needs a restart to change, and max_wal_size trades fewer checkpoints against disk space and recovery time. So change them one at a time and measure the effect of each change.

**Recommendation:** First confirm the values your server is actually running with `SHOW`. Then raise shared_buffers and max_wal_size to fit the machine's RAM and how much it writes, since the defaults are deliberately conservative. Raise work_mem cautiously, ideally for each role or session rather than for the whole server, because its memory use multiplies with the number of operations and connections.

**Research note: picking an analytics side-store next to PostgreSQL**

We're choosing between DuckDB and SQLite as an analytics store that runs alongside our PostgreSQL database. We also need to know whether PostgreSQL 15 supports MERGE. I took all three answers below from official documentation and release notes that I read today.

**DuckDB memory.** DuckDB's configuration reference lists a default `memory_limit` (alias `max_memory`) of 80% of the system's RAM (source: https://duckdb.org/docs/2.0/configuration/overview.html). I first opened https://duckdb.org/docs/stable/configuration/overview, but it only redirects to the 2.0 page above. A process on the same machine as PostgreSQL could therefore try to use most of the host's memory unless we set this limit lower, for example with `SET memory_limit = '4GB'`. On a shared box we should set it explicitly rather than rely on the default.

**SQLite file size.** The SQLite limits page says a database file can hold at most 4,294,967,294 pages. At the largest page size of 65,536 bytes, that comes to about 281 terabytes (source: https://www.sqlite.org/limits.html). The same page says that with the default 4,096-byte page size the limit is about 17.5 terabytes. It also says the 281 TB figure is untested, and that the filesystem's own maximum file size is usually much smaller (source: https://www.sqlite.org/limits.html). For our data volumes, file size is very unlikely to be the deciding factor. The real difference is that SQLite stores data by row and is built for transactions, while DuckDB stores data by column and is built for analytical scans and aggregations.

**MERGE in PostgreSQL.** The PostgreSQL 15.0 release notes list "Support for the SQL MERGE command" among the release highlights. The Utility Commands section describes it as a way "to adjust one table to match another", similar to `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT` but more batch-oriented (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/release/15.0/). So MERGE first shipped in major version 15, and our PostgreSQL 15 servers can use it for upserts, for example when loading data back from the side-store. I did not check later releases. Any MERGE features added after 15 may not be available to us.

**Recommendation.** For an analytics side-store I recommend DuckDB, because its column-based engine suits analytical queries far better than SQLite. We should cap `memory_limit` well below the 80%-of-RAM default so it doesn't compete with PostgreSQL for memory. We can use PostgreSQL 15's MERGE for any batch upserts back into the main database, and keep SQLite in mind only for small transactional or embedded jobs, where its size limits will never matter.

**Research note: TLS versions, DNS label length and HTTP 418**

**TLS 1.3.** TLS 1.3 was first published as RFC 8446, "The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3," a Standards Track document by E. Rescorla from August 2018. Its abstract says it "specifies version 1.3 of the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol" (source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8446). The RFC Editor page for RFC 8446 now marks it obsolete. Its replacement is RFC 9846, which has the same title and is a Proposed Standard with a 2026 copyright notice. The abstract of RFC 9846 says: "This document specifies version 1.3 of the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol" and "This document obsoletes RFC 8446, which specified TLS 1.3" (source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9846). So the current specification for TLS 1.3 is RFC 9846. Older material and vendor documents will usually still cite RFC 8446. The guideline should cite RFC 9846 and mention RFC 8446 as the earlier version, since readers will see both numbers. According to the page summary I read, RFC 9846 also says it obsoletes RFC 5246 (TLS 1.2) and several related RFCs, and updates RFCs 5705 and 6066. Before the guideline relies on that list, someone should check it against the RFC 9846 header (source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9846).

**DNS label length.** A single DNS label can be at most 63 octets. RFC 1035, Section 3.1, explains why: each label starts with a one-octet length field, and the top two bits of that field are reserved. In the RFC's words, "the remaining six bits of the length field limit the label to 63 octets or less" (source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1035). This limit applies to each dot-separated part of a host name, not to the whole name. A naming guideline should state it per label. Host names built automatically, such as names that include service, environment, region or a hash, should be checked against the 63-octet limit for each label.

**HTTP 418 "I'm a teapot".** Status code 418 is "I'm a teapot." It comes from RFC 2324, the Hyper Text Coffee Pot Control Protocol (HTCPCP/1.0), an April Fools' RFC. Section 2.3.2 says: "Any attempt to brew coffee with a teapot should result in the error code '418 I'm a teapot'" (source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2324). RFC 2324 defines it for HTCPCP, not as a standard HTTP status code. I tried to read what the current HTTP semantics specification (RFC 9110) says about 418, but the page was cut off before the relevant section, so I can't confirm its exact wording. Because of that, this note takes no position on 418's status in HTTP itself. That section should be checked before the guideline says anything about it.

**Recommendation.** The guideline should cite RFC 9846 as the current TLS 1.3 specification, note RFC 8446 as the version it replaced, and require that every host-name label be 63 octets or fewer. It should also tell services not to return 418 for real errors and to use the standard HTTP status codes instead, since 418 originates in a joke protocol.
